en.title: O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing
en.author: Charles Wesley
stanzas:
[G]O for a [D]thousand [G]tongues to sing
My [Em]great Re[D7]deem[G]er's praise,
The [G]glories of my [C]God and king,
The [G]triumphs of [D7]His [G]grace!

My gracious master and my God,
Assist me to proclaim,
To spread through all the earth abroad
The honors of Thy name.

Jesus! the name that charms our fears,
That bids our sorrows cease;
'Tis music in the sinner's ears,
'Tis life, and health, and peace.

He breaks the power of canceled sin,
He sets the prisoner free;
His blood can make the foulest clean,
His blood availed for me.

He speaks, and, listening to His voice,
New life the dead receive,
The mournful, broken hearts rejoice,
The humble poor believe.

Hear Him, ye deaf; His praise, ye dumb,
Your loosened tongues employ;
Ye blind, behold your Savior come,
And leap, ye lame, for joy.

Glory to God, and praise and love
Be ever, ever given,
By saints below and saints above,
The church in earth and Heaven.

notes: Wesley's poem runs to eighteen stanzas in the Cyber Hymnal (the familiar opening is verse 7 of the original); shipped here are the six that Trinity Hymnal p.164 prints, in its order, plus the doxological "Glory to God, and praise and love" that most hymnals print last (Cyber Hymnal stanza 8; hymnary's representative text carries it too). Wording is the Cyber Hymnal's throughout -- note Trinity prints "the pow'r of reigning sin" in stanza 4 where the Cyber Hymnal and hymnary have "the power of canceled sin", which is Wesley's. Key G confirmed by the hymnchords.net Trinity chart; hymnary lists AZMON in A-flat, A and G. Chords follow that chart, except that its half cadence at the end of line 2 was resolved to the tonic to keep the strum simple. LYNGHAM and RICHMOND are the other tunes in common use for this text and will not fit this chart. SCANSION: several words are printed full and sung elided -- "power" as "pow'r" (stanza 4), "given" as "giv'n" and "Heaven" as "heav'n" (stanza 7). The Cyber Hymnal prints them full; many hymnals print the elisions. Kept full, as the source has them. VERIFIED 2026-08-02: cross-checked against hymnal.net #163, which agrees on every stanza it shares; the lowercase "my God and king" and "My gracious master" are genuinely the Cyber Hymnal's printing (hymnal.net and most hymnals capitalize both).
